CORE EXPLANATION

References let code access a value without taking ownership. Borrowing rules constrain simultaneous mutable and shared references; lifetime annotations describe relationships, not extend storage.

Borrowing provides references without moving ownership. You may have many immutable `&T` references or one active mutable `&mut T`; conflicting access is rejected to prevent data races. A reference cannot outlive its owner.

Borrowing provides reference access without transferring ownership. Many shared `&T` references or one exclusive `&mut T` may be active, constraining aliasing and data-race risks. A reference cannot outlive its owner, so the compiler rejects dangling references. Slices such as `&str` and `&[T]` view part of a collection without owning it; lifetime annotations describe these relationships rather than creating runtime lifetimes.
